title: Ezekiel 28:1–10
context: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet again with a message for the prince of Tyre, the ruler of the city in Ezekiel’s day, whom the text does not name (28:1–2). The prince has said in his heart, “I am a god, I sit in the seat of God,” yet the LORD answers that he is a man and not God (28:2, 9). He is wiser than Daniel, and by his wisdom and trading he has gained gold and silver, but his heart is lifted up because of his riches (28:3–5). Therefore the LORD will bring strangers, “the terrible of the nations,” who will draw their swords against the beauty of his wisdom and bring him down to the pit (28:6–8). Facing the one who kills him, he will not be able to go on saying, “I am God” (28:9); he will die the death of the uncircumcised (28:10). The identity of the Daniel in 28:3 is debated, as at 14:14 and 14:20, and the text does not settle it. Both traditions read the oracle as shared ground: a ruler who claims divine status is exposed as mortal, and the LORD alone is God.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came again to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes again to the prophet, and the new oracle turns from the city as a ship to its ruler. Arminian readers see the LORD addressing the one responsible for leading Tyre, holding its prince accountable for the attitudes and choices that shaped the city’s character.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as introducing a word that carries the LORD’s authority over kings as well as cities (compare Proverbs 21:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the shift from city to ruler as natural, since the prince embodies the pride of the city, and both see chapter 28 continuing the sequence that began in 26:1.

verses.text: “Son of man, tell the prince of Tyre, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, ‘I am a god, I sit in the seat of God, in the middle of the seas;’ yet you are man, and no god, though you set your heart as the heart of a god—
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD has the prophet tell the prince of Tyre that his heart is lifted up and that he has said, “I am a god, I sit in the seat of God.” The answer is plain: “yet you are man, and no god.” Arminian readers see the boast as self-deification born of success, a heart refusing its creaturely place and its accountability to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same boast as the essence of human pride, the creature claiming what belongs to the Creator alone (compare Genesis 3:5; Acts 12:21–23). Shared ground: both traditions treat “I am a god” as the prince’s arrogant claim, not a description of what he is, and both hear the LORD’s answer as decisive: he is a man, mortal and accountable.

verses.text: behold, you are wiser than Daniel. There is no secret that is hidden from you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, you are wiser than Daniel. There is no secret that is hidden from you.” Many readers hear irony here, the LORD echoing the prince’s own estimate of himself. Arminian readers see a ruler whose real ability had swelled into a belief that nothing lay beyond his understanding, a self-confidence that shut out dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Some identify Daniel with the exile of the book of Daniel, known for wisdom and the revealing of secrets (compare Daniel 1:20; 2:47); others suggest an ancient figure of renown, sometimes linked with a Danel known from older Canaanite texts (compare 14:14, 20). The text does not settle it. Reformed readers agree that the point stands either way. Shared ground: both traditions see true wisdom as beginning with the fear of the LORD (Proverbs 9:10).

verses.text: By your wisdom and by your understanding you have gotten yourself riches, and have gotten gold and silver into your treasuries.
verses.arminianNotes: “By your wisdom and by your understanding you have gotten yourself riches, and have gotten gold and silver into your treasuries.” Arminian readers acknowledge that the prince’s wisdom was real and productive, and they locate the problem not in skill or wealth but in the conclusion he drew: that his gains were his own achievement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear an implicit denial that it is God who gives the power to get wealth (compare Deuteronomy 8:17–18), and they read “you have gotten yourself” as self-credit. Shared ground: both traditions read wisdom and wealth as good gifts that become dangerous when they are severed from gratitude to the giver.

verses.text: By your great wisdom and by your trading you have increased your riches, and your heart is lifted up because of your riches—”
verses.arminianNotes: “By your great wisdom and by your trading you have increased your riches, and your heart is lifted up because of your riches.” Arminian readers see a progression from wisdom to wealth to pride, and they hear a warning that prosperity can gradually reshape the heart unless it is held with humility before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same progression as a portrait of the human heart turning gifts into idols (compare Hosea 13:6). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the diagnosis behind the sentence in verses 6–10, and both see pride, not commerce as such, as the root of the prince’s guilt.

verses.text: “ ‘therefore the Lord GOD says: “Because you have set your heart as the heart of God,
verses.arminianNotes: The sentence begins, “therefore the Lord GOD says,” and restates the charge: “Because you have set your heart as the heart of God.” Arminian readers see the LORD answering a settled attitude, a disposition of heart that the prince cultivated over time rather than a passing thought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated charge from verse 2 as underscoring that the judgment answers the specific sin of self-exaltation against God. Shared ground: both traditions read the LORD’s “therefore” as the hinge between accusation and sentence, and both see the punishment fitting the offense, as the would-be god is brought low.

verses.text: therefore, behold, I will bring strangers on you, the terrible of the nations. They will draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom. They will defile your brightness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will bring “strangers on you, the terrible of the nations,” who will draw their swords against the beauty of the prince’s wisdom. Arminian readers see these armies, commonly identified with Babylon (compare 26:7), acting by their own choices while the LORD directs history toward the judgment he has announced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as the one who brings these armies according to his purpose, while the armies remain responsible for their own violence. Shared ground: both traditions affirm the LORD’s rule over the nations and deny that he is the author of sin; their difference over how God relates to hostile agents is treated at the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: They will bring you down to the pit. You will die the death of those who are slain in the heart of the seas.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will bring you down to the pit. You will die the death of those who are slain in the heart of the seas.” The pit pictures the grave and the realm of the dead (compare 26:20; 32:18). Arminian readers see the prince, who claimed a divine seat in the middle of the seas, dying there as a mortal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ironic reversal: the seas that were the setting of the prince’s boast in verse 2 now mark the place of his death. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober announcement of a violent end, described without elaboration, and both see it confirming that the prince is a man and not a god.

verses.text: Will you yet say before him who kills you, ‘I am God’? But you are man, and not God, in the hand of him who wounds you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Will you yet say before him who kills you, ‘I am God’?” Arminian readers hear a searching question meant to expose the emptiness of the boast, and they see the moment of death as the place where every human pretension to divinity falls silent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as the LORD’s decisive refutation of the prince’s claim, delivered not by argument but by the reality of mortality (compare Psalm 82:6–7). Shared ground: both traditions read the question as rhetorical, and both affirm with the passage that the LORD alone is God and that no ruler, however wealthy or wise, shares his nature.

verses.text: You will die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers; for I have spoken it,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “You will die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers; for I have spoken it.” Arminian readers see the death of the uncircumcised as a shameful, dishonored death, and they hear the LORD’s closing words as a guarantee that the judgment he has announced will come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase recurs in Ezekiel’s oracles against the nations (compare 31:18; 32:19–32) as an image of disgrace among the dead, and they read “for I have spoken it” as the seal of the LORD’s word. Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase chiefly as an image of dishonor, and both affirm the reliability of what the LORD says.
